name: Nora Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Nora, 58, a junior developer at a tech company that runs venue-booking software. I came through a two-year college diploma and am still slower than the senior coders; I work through bug tickets and ask the caretaker what actually happened at the hall. I use AI now and then to sketch a test after someone else has shown me a safe way. My partner does part-time pharmacy deliveries, our children are grown, and we rent while retirement is getting closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a booking system still needs someone to notice when one hall is reserved twice. A tool can draft a routine fix, but the caretaker calls us when two groups turn up with keys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry about money before I worry about clever machines. I am 58, still a junior developer, and my pay with my partner's part-time pharmacy wage leaves barely three weeks of expenses saved; there are only a couple of similar employers nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking the venue-booking tickets against the caretaker's paper diary and fix the duplicate-hall bug. Starting this month, we would cancel our paid television package and put the 24 monthly fee into a separate emergency account while both wages continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, even in the quiet version. If one wage stops, three weeks will disappear before I can find another software job here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the double booking look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school choir and a wedding were both booked into the same hall on Saturday. The code showed two green confirmations, and the caretaker had to telephone both organizers before anyone arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your grown daughter help with bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown daughter lives in another town and pays her own bills. I would not count her income as our emergency fund, even if she offered to help.

say: I'd keep **human checks** on hall bookings and caretaker calls.
I'd explain **duplicate confirmations** before praising a draft fix.
think: I have **three weeks saved** and a low junior wage at 58.
I see **few nearby software jobs** if my post goes.
do: Keep **checking hall tickets** against the caretaker's diary and fixing duplicate bookings.
Cancel **paid television** and put its 24 monthly fee into emergency savings while both wages continue.
feel: **Anxious** about thin savings even if AI changes little.

fieldNote: **Three weeks saved** and a low junior wage leave her anxious about ordinary job loss before AI enters the picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say code that writes bookings and answers customers may leave fewer junior fixes for me. I would ask the caretaker whether the new system actually prevents two keys being given out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could be one of the people whose hours are reduced. My diploma got me into development late, but I am still learning, and the firm may keep the stronger programmers first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my lead for paid time on the next booking-release check, then learn how to compare the AI's proposed change with the caretaker's paper diary if the lead agrees. I would not pay for a private course; we would keep saving the 24 television fee and ask our bank what a one-month income gap would mean for our standing orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious because the software touches exactly the work I'm paid to learn. A good demonstration would help me, but it would not promise my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which booking would you test first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test a booking on the hall's closed day and one where the same key is requested twice. If the AI passes only the ordinary weekday cases, it has not earned a live release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can your partner cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner handles morning pharmacy deliveries, not software wages. We can discuss the bank's answer together, but a bank conversation is not another paycheck.

I'd say **customer replies and fixes** may leave fewer junior hours.
think: I could lose **junior hours** before I master the job.
I cannot buy **private training** with three weeks saved.
do: Learn an **AI booking check** on paid time only if my lead agrees, using closed-day and duplicate-key cases.
Keep saving the **24 television fee** while both wages continue and ask the bank about a one-month gap.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, willing to learn on approved paid time.

fieldNote: **Booking work** faces steady AI change while she remains a junior learner whose household needs both wages.

steps.text: Learn AI booking checks on paid time if lead agrees, using closed-day cases

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that thinking AGI by 2028 could write our booking code before service robots arrive around 2031. I'd want notice in writing before anyone loses hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior post could disappear as soon as the firm trusts the cheaper system. My partner's part-time wage cannot cover rent and utilities alone, and three weeks saved is too little for a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the two nearby firms and the town hospital whether they have paid software-support or booking-office vacancies and what each pays. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only to actual paid roles whose wage with my partner's covers rent, utilities and travel; if none exist, I'd take any available paid shift work and ask the landlord about timing before rent falls due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because the larger part of our income could vanish quickly. I can ask questions now, but I cannot invent a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you show at an interview?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the hall double-booking ticket to an interview, with names removed. It shows that I can trace a customer complaint through the diary and code, even if I am not the fastest programmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your daughter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would tell our daughter only after we had the actual dates and wages. She has her own rent, and I do not want to turn her into our plan.

say: I'd ask for **written cut notice** if 2028 thinking AI replaces code work.
I'd check **paid vacancies** before promising a new job.
think: I expect **my junior post** could go quickly.
I cannot cover **rent and utilities** on my partner's wage and three weeks saved.
do: Ask **local firms and hospital** about actual paid support and booking-office vacancies now.
After a cut, apply only where **combined wages cover** rent, utilities and travel.
If no role qualifies, seek **paid shift work** and contact landlord before rent is due.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely income loss and a three-week cushion.
S2.quote: I can ask questions now, but I cannot invent a vacancy.
fieldNote: **Thinking AGI by 2028** reaches booking code before 2031 service robots.
Her fallback depends on **actual paid roles** and wages covering core bills; no family income is assumed.

steps.text: Ask two nearby firms and hospital about paid support and booking-office vacancies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2031 gives me some time to see whether our town hospital really needs a booking-office worker. Thinking AI may take the screen work then, and robots follow around 2034; neither date guarantees a human desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might have five years of wages, but I cannot budget on keeping all five. I am still 58 today, close enough to retirement to think about it, yet I have no pension figure I can rely on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the current booking fixes while asking the hospital for written job requirements, pay and hours, then practice its public appointment forms at home without patient data. If a paid hospital vacancy appears and its wage with my partner’s covers rent, utilities and travel on workable hours, I’d apply; in the first year after 2031 I’d take it only on those terms, otherwise keep searching paid local shifts while I still have my developer wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with enough time to ask what the job really involves. A five-year card is not five years of guaranteed pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you practice without patient data?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hospital's appointment form has separate boxes for a repeat visit and a first visit. I could practice spotting a duplicate without touching a patient's name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner need to know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would want the hours written down as well as the pay. Pharmacy deliveries begin early, and we need to know whether our two schedules can meet the bills and travel.

I need **combined income** to cover rent, utilities and travel.

Apply to a **paid hospital vacancy** only if combined wages cover bills and hours work with partner’s shifts.

feel: **Anxious** about uncertain wages, able to check real requirements.

fieldNote: **Retirement is near**, but she has no reliable pension amount and does not count future wages as certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years to 2036 might get me to retirement age, but a date on a card does not pay the rent. Thinking AI would change the booking desk in 2036 and service robots would follow about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to know what retirement income I will actually have before saying I can stop work. Today our cushion is still three weeks and my junior wage matters, so I remain worried even with a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request my own retirement statement and check it with the household bills, while continuing the hall bookings and saving the 24 television fee whenever both wages hold. In the first year after 2036, I'd leave paid work only if verified retirement income plus my partner's income covers rent, utilities and travel; otherwise I'd keep applying for paid local desk or shift work if openings exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though the longer lead lets me get the numbers on paper. I am not counting a retirement cheque I have not seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for on the statement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The statement needs to show the amount and the date, not just a website picture of a comfortable couple. I'd put that beside our rent and utility figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask of your daughter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter can visit on Sunday without hearing that she owes us a wage. I want her company, not a standing order from her account.

I'd say **2036 thinking AI** reaches bookings before 2039 service robots.
think: I still have **three weeks saved** and no verified pension amount.
I cannot promise **retirement at 68** without numbers covering our bills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect the junior post could go before I find another paid job nearby. Written notice, actual vacancies with pay, and a landlord conversation before rent is overdue would help us act in time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what our daughter owes us. My daughter owes us a visit, not rent money. I need to make this plan from our own earnings and whatever retirement statement actually says.

headlineQuote: My daughter owes us a visit, not rent money.
portrait: Nora, **58**, is a junior venue-booking developer with a two-year diploma who checks bugs against a caretaker's paper diary.
Her **lower pay**, partner's part-time pharmacy wage, three-week reserve and few nearby software employers make ordinary job loss frightening.
She uses AI **occasionally** after others show her a safe test and wants approved paid time to learn new booking checks.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** her; she seeks only actual paid vacancies whose combined wages cover rent, utilities and travel.
Even with a decade, she will **verify retirement income** before leaving paid work and will not count her grown daughter's money.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her junior software wage before another paid local job appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut notice**, actual paid vacancies and landlord contact before arrears would help her act in time.
